utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, may we have -- would you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Matthew Olmsted for the Prosecution; joined by Case Manager, Thomas Laugel; and our intern, Simona Onicel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the next witness be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness. First of all, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot hear any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. I'll repeat the question. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you please tell us your name, and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Aleksandar Vasiljevic, the 8th of July, 1938.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasiljevic. You are about to make the solemn declaration by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I must point out to you that by doing so, you expose yourself to the penalties of perjury should you give false or untruthful information to the Tribunal. Could I now ask you to make the solemn declaration the usher will give to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated. Mr. Olmsted, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, General Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to begin by asking you a few questions about your written statement. Did you provide a written statement to the ICTY Office of the Prosecution which you signed on the 19th of April, 2013?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 6444 on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: General, can you confirm that this is your statement.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now prior to testifying here today, did you have an opportunity to review this statement?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And during proofing this past weekend, did you identify a few corrections to this statement?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I would like to go through those corrections at this point. If we could turn to paragraph 14 of your statement. And actually I'd like to turn to the end of this paragraph which deals with general structural issues. And I'm interested only in the last sentence of this paragraph, which is an incomplete sentence. Says, "In response" -- I'm sorry, it says, "In practice, the secretary ...," and then it doesn't continue on from there. Can we just delete the sentence, General?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we can because the continuation doesn't really matter, who General Kadijevic contacted directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to paragraph 52 of the statement which in the English version, is on page 19. General, the second sentence reads: "In response, the Serbian population in Croatia began to arm themselves in an organised manner in the latter part of 1991, albeit to a lesser degree than the Croats." Can you be more precise as to when in 1991 the Serb population began arming themselves in an organised manner?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: This is about arming in organised fashion. That was not in the latter half of 1991 but, rather, in the first half of that year, after the session of the Presidency of the SFRY that took place on the 12th of March, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could now turn to paragraph 134 of the statement, and this is on page 49 of the English version. And, General, this is not a correction for you but, rather, for -- for the record and for the Trial Chamber. With regard to this paragraph, we would like to revise the reference to 65 ter Exhibit 456, and make it a reference, instead, to 65 ter Exhibit 443. Exhibit 443 is an identical version of Exhibit 456 and it has already been admitted into evidence as P1727. If we could turn to paragraph 138. This is on page 50 of the English version. General Vasiljevic, this paragraph relates to a meeting you attended with General Kadijevic. Could you let us now, do you have a clarification to make with regard to this particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I stated in my statement that I was in Vukovar five times, and one of those visits to Vukovar was the one on the 16th of November. However, I didn't go to Vukovar on that occasion because the meeting with General Kadijevic and the generals in the field did not take place in Vukovar but, rather, in Dalj. So I was in Vukovar four times in fact, and once I was at Dalj.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you give us the names of the other participants in that meeting other than you and General Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: With General Kadijevic, there was the inner circle of the staff. And from the field, there were the local commanders: General Zivota Panic; General Mandaric, the commander of the TO; General Biorcevic, the commander of the Novi Sad Corps; General Mico Delic, the commander of the Guards Division; General -- or, at the time he was still a colonel, Mrksic, commander of the Guard Brigade and commander of OG South. These are the persons that I remember having attended the meeting. I don't think there were any others.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to paragraph 165 which, in the English version, is on page 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, General, this is a paragraph that relates to the collection centres in Serbia. And about midway through the statement, it states that on 16 December 1991 that you toured Stajicevo and Begejci collection centres; is that correct? Did you tour both collection centres on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No. On the 16th of December, I went to Stajicevo with General Simon Timunov [phoen], and the security organs from the operative team who did operational work at the collection centres briefed us. They also reported about the work with the detained persons there and at Begejci. I did not go to Begejci, though, but I have notes about it. I was at Stajicevo but I did not go to Begejci.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And could you clarify who was the head of the operative team at Stajicevo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: The operative team of the security organ at Stajicevo was headed by Lieutenant-Colonel Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And was Lieutenant-Colonel Zivanovic present during your tour of Stajicevo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: He was at Stajicevo at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could go to paragraph 167. This is on the next page, page 61. And we see midway through the paragraph, it reads: "There were a total of 1.300 Croat prisoners held at this facility." Could you tell us which facility you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: The facility is the collection centre at Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we can go to paragraph 168, which begins the bottom of page 61 and, actually, I'm interested in -- towards the end of the paragraph on page 62. And, General, this is another correction that I don't need any answer from you. It's for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is a typographical error in the English version of the last sentence. The last name of the individual referenced in the last sentence should be "Cvek," C-v-e-k, rather than "Crk," C-r-k.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Finally, if we could turn to paragraph 169, which is on page 62 of the English. General Vasiljevic, in this paragraph you describe a meeting that you attended at the Sremska Mitrovica KP Dom with Goran Hadzic and his delegation. And you provide the date of that meeting as 10 December 1991. Is that the correct date of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: The persons mentioned from the SAO really were at the collection centre of Sremska Mitrovica on the 10th of December. However, on that day, I did not contact these persons. I had no contact with them because, on that day, I took part in the exchange of a group of detained persons from the Sremska Mitrovica collection centre. That group -- in that group, there was Vesna Bosanac. In other words, I wasn't at the collection centre on that day. The conversation I had was with Colonel Jugoslav Maksimovic, who was head of the operative team. When I reviewed my notebooks, I established that on the 13th of October, 1991, I was at the Sremska Mitrovica collection centre where the military prosecutor called a meeting with the security organ from the operative team, and my contact with Goran Hadzic and those other persons, according to my notes, took place on the 13th of December. That would be a correction of this text.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So this paragraph relates to your meeting with Goran Hadzic on the 13th of December; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we will talk about the meeting on the 10th of December later on during your testimony. But with the corrections and clarifications that we have just made to your statement, are you satisfied that the information is accurate and correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: It is correct and accurate to the extent my memory is. I refreshed it by reviewing my notes from the time. So I stand by this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you were asked about these matters contained in your statement, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: On the whole, essentially it would -- it would tally with what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point, we would like to tender in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we clarify what does it mean "essentially"?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: General Vasiljevic, could you clarify that? As this is a important part of admitting your statement into evidence, what did you mean essentially your answers would be the same?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: This statement is 60-odd pages long. Now, whoever expects that I can recite all this by heart, word for word, I don't think anybody could do that. But I said that the essential matters which I'm -- because of which I'm here to testify, I stand by, and there are no problems with them. And, for the record and in order to avoid any confusion, I stand by my statement fully, and if I were to be asked any questions about these elements, I would give the same answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution would tender into evidence 65 ter Exhibit 6444, under seal, and we've already uploaded a redacted version of the witness's statement as 65 ter Exhibit 6444.1 for the reasons specified in the underlying motion with regard to this statement. There are also a number of associated exhibits, several which have already been admitted into evidence, including some recently and we would seek the unadmitted ones to be admitted into evidence. And finally with regard to one of the associated exhibits, it's 65 ter 495, it's incorrectly indicated on the exhibit list as not being subject to protective measures. It is in fact subject to protective measures as it falls within the redacted portions of this witness's statement. And therefore we ask that that exhibit be tendered under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You have all that, Madam Registrar? Then we can admit and mark them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The statement will become Exhibit P2913 and the redacted version is P2913.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: General Vasiljevic, although it's covered in your statement, just for the record, if you could please provide your rank as well as the position you held in the 1991/1992 time-period.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I was Major-General of the Yugoslav People's Army at the time, and I was a chief of the intelligence administration -- or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Security Administration of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And as chief of the Security Administration, who was your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: The federal secretary of national defence, General Veljko Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I will now ask you a series of questions that clarify, expand upon a number of matters that are raised in your written statement. And, first of all, in paragraphs 42 to 46 of your statement, you describe the JNA's jurisdiction over crimes and disciplinary infractions and I would like to -- you to look at a few documents that may shed further light on this particular issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have on e-court, 65 ter 407. This is tab 77.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this is a report by the security organ of the guards Motorised Brigade to the security organ of the SSNO dated 12 October 1991. If we can could just turn to the last page for a moment? General, could you tell us, who drafted this report?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: This report is handwritten by, as we can see at the end, Captain First Class Mladen Karan, who was assistant for counter-intelligence in the security section of the guards brigade at the head of which there was Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you explain to us why this report would be submitted directly to the SSNO?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that you were not precise when you said who this report was submitted to. It was not submitted directly to the SSNO. There was a procedure in place and according to that procedure it was submitted to the chief of the security organ in the office of the federal secretary of national defence. The Guards Brigade was not subordinated to General Kadijevic but rather to the head of his office who, at the time, was General Vuk Obradovic. In the office to which the brigade was subordinated, there is a security section so that the chief of security at brigade level and his deputy, this captain first class, submitted the report not to the Security Administration but rather to the chief of security at the secretary's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. If we could turn to page 2 of the original, page 1 of the English. The author of this report discusses the work of the security organs in interviewing captured members of the ZNG regarding the situation within their formation. And if we look towards the bottom of the page in both versions he writes: "Also being verified is the information on individual who took part in the crimes against the local population and JNA members and whose actions can be qualified as war crimes." He then writes: "Other prisoners are handed over to the local organs of authority after identification, in other words, to the Territorial Defence Staff and the police force for further steps to be taken." First, General, when it's referred to as "other prisoners," do you read that as referring to prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there are no other prisoners. There are prisoners and there are detainees. These are prisoners, that is to say, person who were in paramilitary units and other than illegal units of the Republic of Croatia, and, well, this is a rather lengthy text, but the essence of the question is: How this selection was carried out of these persons who were arrested. Security organs interviewed the person who had been taken prisoner. As far as can I see here, they singled out 25 persons as suspected of having committed either crimes or actually the crime of armed rebellion, according to the laws that were then in force. These persons remained under the jurisdiction of the military organs. These other persons who did not have such status were handed over, as far as I know now, to a type of collections centre that the Territorial Defence had at the Velepromet facility. One of the main persons there was some Ljubinko. Maybe I will remember his last name. As for a these other persons, these 25, according to procedure, they were supposed to be handed over to the collection centre in Begejci that dealt with the problem of persons who had taken part in the armed rebellion and who had been suspected of having committed crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you tell us under the procedures that existed back in 1991, when was it appropriate to turn over prisoners of war to the local authorities?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, there were TO units of the SAO Slavonia. They had their staff in Vukovar. And since these were person who had been taken prisoner, they had to be put up somewhere for the purposes of further procedure. For security organs, it was persons who were suspected of having committed more serious crimes were of interest. As far as I know, they stayed at this collection centre in Velepromet. Now what the procedure was later followed in respect of them, I don't know. I imagine that they were also subjected to some kind of a triage, and I assume that some persons were released and also some were used for exchanges at the time. Because, at these local levels, in the first stage, there were exchanges that were not in accordance with the orders of the Federal Secretariat for a national defence and then General Blagoje Adzic wrote a special order prohibiting local exchanges because at the federal secretary for national defence there was a special organ for the civilian sector. That's what it was called. And it was headed by General Nikola Pujic and he was the assistant federal secretary for the civilian section. Within his organisational unit a special commission had been set up for the exchange of detained and imprisoned persons in order to prevent these local exchanges that were at brigade level or at even lower levels, with -- so these exchanges with local commanders of the other side an order was issued that this be halted and that things be done in accordance with the regulations that I referred to just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2914, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: General, since you raised the issue of exchanges, if we could have 65 ter 5999 on the e-court. This is tab 214. This is a memorandum from the 12th Corps, committee for monitoring cease-fire date 30 September 1991. And if I could focus your attention on the second paragraph, it is reported that a meeting was held in Klisa with a three-member EU mission which was attended by Colonel Boro Ivanovic, Colonel Vujica Rakicevic and two ministers of -- from the SBWS government on the Serb side and then a former lieutenant-colonel on the Croatian side. And the topic was exchanges of those captured. You referred to a moment ago a procedure that existed before exchange was regulated by the SSNO. Is this an example of that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is an illustration of what you referred to just now. Here, we can see that other part that I spoke of a moment ago, and that is to say that two representatives of the SAO Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem took part in this exchange too; which is to say that they had -- well, shall I put it this way, their own prisoners too who went for an exchange because these were only prisoners who were under the jurisdiction and control of the JNA. There wouldn't have been any need for these persons to take part in this, unless they had some prisoners of their own. And, in practice, on the ground, that is what happened; namely, that the Territorial Defence had a collection centre of their own and a location where they kept persons who were prisoners and who they interrogated and who could then go for exchanges and follow judicial or other procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2915, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: General, I want to return to the issue of jurisdiction over crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could have on e-court Exhibit P1865.1. This is tab 134.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is an information report from the SSNO Security Administration dated 26 May 1992. General, were you still head of the Security Administration when this report was issued?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I was not. I was pensioned off on the 8th of May, 1992. I see here the form of this information that does match the form of documents that were in place at the time when I was head of the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 3 in both versions. And if we could focus in on the -- I believe it's the fourth paragraph. It's the one with the exclamation points in the margin. And there's reference to a Security Administration report dated 26 October 1991. And from the paragraphs above that, we can see that that report pertain to crimes committed in Lovas during this period. Could you tell us, what report are they referring to?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: There 's a reference here to something that was written on the 26th of October. However, I remember for sure that the information that was compiled about the crimes in the village of Lovas that was submitted for nine persons: Four generals at the SSNO, commander of the Territorial Defence of Serbia, the Ministry of Defence of Serbia, and the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia, and the attorney-general for the JNA, at that time it was Mladen Papic. This information was strictly confidential 590 and this was the 25th of October. I received the first information - if I'm supposed to speak about that now - about what happened -- or, rather, what was established later to have been a crime in the village of Lovas. On the 23rd or 24th of October, I think, the chief of security at the 1st Military District, and this, as far as I can see on this page, this is a survey of all the cases that had occurred and that had to do with war crimes. And specifically with regard to this passage here, there is a reference to -- actually not all the persons that this information was submitted to had been mentioned, the under-secretary of the SDB for the MUP of Serbia, and it was submitted to the minister of the interior, this information of the 25th, that I referred to just now. And, also, it just says here that it was submitted to three addresses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you submit -- or did the SSNO Security Administration submit this report to the civilian prosecutor in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, because it was submitted to the military prosecutor of the JNA, and he was fully informed about this event. Although he thought that the civilian prosecutor should have been informed -- or, rather, had he believed that it was necessary to inform the civilian prosecutor, he would have done so through official channels. However, the important thing is that the information was submitted to the organs of the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Serbia that also have certain obligations vis-a-vis the Office of the Prosecutor in Serbia. So in that information there is a reference to four military persons and eight civilian persons for a whom it was actually the MUP of Serbia that had jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: As a general practice, did the JNA security organs file criminal reports directly with civilian prosecutors?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2 of this report. In the first paragraph, the report states that the JNA security organs gathered operative and other information on serious criminal acts committed by volunteer formations who were, for the most part, on the strength of the SBWS TO. The report then states that these crimes were generally only registered and only partially documented and provides as -- as one explanation for this the "non-existence of the legally enforceable jurisdiction." How do you interpret that, "the non-existence of the legally enforceable jurisdiction."

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the question is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. I'll repeat it then. Can you see where it says in this first paragraph that -- they explain that they only partially documented some of these crimes? And only registered them? And then it provides as one of the bases for this that there was a non-existence of the legally enforceable jurisdiction. And my question is: Could you explain what is meant by that, the "non-existence of the legally enforceable jurisdiction"?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see that here in e-court. Now, what is all this about? Organs of military security, organs of the military police and other official organs, at any level, objectively have jurisdiction in terms of crimes that the military court is in charge of. And that is chapter 25 of the then-Criminal Code. So all powers and the entire procedure is enforced in terms of perpetrators who fall under military courts. If these are crimes that the military court is not in charge of and if they find out the crime had been committed that a crime that a civilian court is supposed to deal with, then, in accordance to general legal provisions, they were supposed to secure the scene, collect at least initial knowledge -- information and inform either the military prosecutor or the military commander, and then he provides information to the persons who have territorial jurisdiction; namely, that they should take over these cases and fully follow the procedure involved. That is why there is their note of theirs that this is partially documented. However, it was submitted. Rather, this information was submitted to the MUPs in the territory that were in charge. And I can give several examples now, but let me not take up too much of your time. Say, the 28th of November, where the organs of the military police at the farm in Lovas found 20-something corpses, some of which had been massacred, and they immediately documented this by photographs and informed the MUP, so that they could follow the full procedure because there was nothing that indicated that it was military personnel who had committed that crime. It was perpetrators unknown that were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if the perpetrators are unknown, who has jurisdiction over that crime?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would say that both sides are informed. That is to say, both sides have to work on that, namely, to search for the perpetrators who are unknown. However, if the said crime is under the jurisdiction of the civilian authorities, then, it is the organs of the civilian sector that should pursue the matter. Military organs can co-operate from a certain point of view; namely, if there are several indications that a military person had committed the crimes involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we read further on an in this paragraph, it states: "All information was immediately passed on to the local organs of government, the organs of internal affairs of the Republic of Serbia, and the military legal organs." With regard to crimes committed by paramilitaries who were under the strength of the SBWS TO, was that the general practice?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would object to the question in the last sentence. Because it is a leading question and there is no foundation laid for the paramilitaries under the strength of the SBWS.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I was actually referring to -- further above this passage, it does mention serious committed by volunteer formations who were for the most part on the strength of the SBWS TO. And my question is simply whether it was the general practice for the security organs to submit information regarding these kind of crimes to the local organs of authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You still object, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: General Vasiljevic, do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And these local territorial organs were informed because then, when this happened, there was a local police station, there was a staff of the Territorial Defence of the SAO Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I think you touched on this briefly, but what was the procedure if a criminal report that was within the civilian court's jurisdiction was filed with the military prosecutor's office? Was there a process that it went through?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: There is co-operation too, but, first, and foremost there is this obligation on the part of the prosecutor's office and other state organs. Namely, that if they receive information for which they establish that they do not have jurisdiction, then they should forward that information to the organ that is in charge. So the military prosecutor receives information that he does not have jurisdiction for because it's not chapter 25, that is to say, crimes against the armed forces, then he hands over this information to the court or the prosecutor or some other state organ and that was in charge. And it works the other way around too.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have D17.1 on the screen. This is tab 135.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this is an analysis by the State Security Department, Belgrade, of information received from SSNO Security Administration dated 27 May 1992, and this appears to be in relation to the document we just looked at. And if we look under item 1, it's relating to the crimes committed in Lovas in October 1991. And if we could turn the page in both versions, we see at the end of the paragraph, item 1, it states -- or it concludes: "We think that the military prosecutor would have the authority for the possible criminal procedure against these persons." That is, the -- the perpetrators of the crimes in Lovas. Do you agree with that conclusion, General?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I could not agree with that because, as for this incident, first of all, it was members of a paramilitary organisation that were involved, Dusan Silni. Before that, they committed other crimes, too, in addition to the one that is referred to here. Also they were suspected of having taken part in this in a certain way. It was four military persons who were suspects. I filed criminal reports against these four to the military prosecutor for the JNA. However, since there were eight other civilians here from the paramilitary detachment Dusan Silni, it was only natural that since these were civilians and the victims were civilians, it was only natural that civilian organs should also initiate a procedure with regard to the matter. Afterward there could be co-ordination between the two prosecutors who is actually supposed to act, because preceding could be brought before a military court, too, if there is responsibility of these four military persons and also jurisdiction can be transferred so that civilians could be tried before a military court as well and it works the other way around too. If the civilian court would be trying all of these people, then in some occasions the law allows for military personnel to be tried before civilian courts too. I read this information. The first information that you showed me, that military information, where there is a reference to all the crimes that were committed in the territory for a certain period of time. Now this, what I'm being shown now is a MUP document and there is an analysis here. It doesn't say who this was submitted to. At any rate, I shall take the liberty of saying that this is a case of shifting blame or avoiding any situation where one would be held guilty. They say, Well, it was the military, it was the army that was in charge of all that. Whereas, they provide a describe of events that show that civilians were responsible too. And now there is the question immediately as to why these four military personnel immediately faced proceedings before a military court of law whereas those who, indeed, took part in these killings and in the mistreatment of civilians, torture of civilians. Before this incident in Lovas, they were not arrested at all and they were not part of any kind of judicial procedure until this case was reopened before the court in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And that case that was reopened in the court in Belgrade, do you recall exactly when that was, what year?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I think it's an adjudicated case and it was in 2007 or 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: General, just to wrap of the issue of jurisdiction over crimes. Could you tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just to wrap up the issue, General, of jurisdiction over crimes. Could you tell us just briefly what was the effect of a declaration of an immediate threat of war on the JNA's jurisdiction over crimes?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the declaration of an immediate threat of war was made in early October 1991. I believe it was the 3rd of October. I dare not to interpret what changes and what comes into effect once such a declaration is made. But I know what happened. In late August and early September, the JNA was supposed to release a large number of soldiers or -- serving their mandatory military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you, General. In fact, I might want to come back to this issue of mobilisation later on, but I really just want to focus on jurisdictional issue, criminal jurisdiction issues. And my question is simply: With a declaration of an immediate threat of war, did that have any impact on the JNA's criminal jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And under the criminal procedures that would exist during an immediate threat of war, how long could a criminal suspect be detained without a court order?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Under normal circumstances in peacetime, people could be detained up to 24 hours. Under the -- in some cases up to 72 hours. Under extraordinary conditions and when the state of war is declared, some more stringent rules applied. In 1991, no decree had been passed changing the previous status regarding the authorities and powers of official organs. So detention could last up to 72 hours. This boils down to the fact that the -- the -- the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I apologise, General Vasiljevic, but we're going to need you to repeat the last bit of your answer because the interpreters did not pick it up. And perhaps speak a little bit slower so that they can catch it.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I'll do my best. The extraordinary circumstances in this -- that situation of the immediate threat of war had no repercussions with respect to the change of the legal provisions in force in peacetime. In extraordinary circumstances, especially in war time these authorities can be transferred and detention could be extended up to 30 days. When the state of war is declared, with respect to the aggression in Kosovo, the security organs had the power to detain persons up to 30 days. This was based on a special decree. However, in this case, no other decree was passed except the one about general mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Beginning at paragraph 69 of your statement, you describe information that was available to the Security Administration concerning various Serb volunteer and paramilitary units that were operating in the SBWS region in 1991 and 1992. And I'd like to show you a couple of reports to see if you can assist in authenticating them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I apologise, but I think this should be done in private session as it does relate to matters that are redact the in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, my next exhibit is a video, and I think it's going to go beyond four minutes. Perhaps we can take our break at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Olmsted. General Vasiljevic, this is the time for our first break. We take 30 minutes and come back at 11.00. The Court Usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: While the witness is being brought in, may I state for the record that we are joined by Alex Demirdjian. And may I also state for the record that two weeks ago, Alex and Evelyn had a new addition to their family. Their daughter Sarah was born.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Congratulations, Mr. Demirdjian. Two weeks ago, you said? When was that exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Your Honours. On the 20th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just a few days after the birth of my fourth grandchild.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you for Mr. Olmsted for his kind words and Your Honour's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: General Vasiljevic, before we resume, I will do my best not to cut you off. However, if I feel that you are going beyond the scope of my question, I might have to do that, just for the reason that I want to make sure that I cover all of the material with you. I do not by any means intends to be rude by doing so. Let's return to your statement. Now, in paragraph 76 of your statement, you discuss the Serbian Volunteer Guard Unit operating in the SBWS under the command of Zeljko Raznjatovic. And according -- could you tell us, according to the information that was available to the Security Administration, to whom was Arkan's units subordinate?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Arkan's units -- unit, as far as Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem is concerned, objectively speaking, was under the jurisdiction of Radovan Stojicic, Badza. It appeared in several places, and from time to time, some of the military officers, commanders were in contact with him, like General Biorcevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And during this period, what position did Badza hold?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Badza, as a member of the MUP of Serbia, in 1991, was sent to Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem and he was, in fact, the commander of all these local units in the territory of Baranja and Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was he given a particular title within the SBWS?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about any official title. But he was the dominant person there who, in fact, had the greatest authority, authority behind which the president of the Republic of Serbia stood. And he was a man who had a decisive say for everything regarding these units. From time to time, he took part in -- meetings with General Zivota Panic, and some problems were being sorted out there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did he have a relationship with regard to the SBWS TO?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was in contact with Mr. Goran Hadzic too. Practically he was the commander of all these units, but officially he was not commander of the staff of the Territorial Defence in Vukovar 's [indiscernible] Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. These were other persons. He was a man who had his own staff, as far as I can remember, in Borovo Naselje, and, in fact, all these units were subordinated to him. So he had such power that he could remove people, move them from one place to another, engage them, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I would like to show you a series of video-clips this is 65 ter 4991.6. And the video-clip is quite short. It's only five seconds. And it's, I think, page 1 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "You know that we are under the command of the Territorial Defence of the Serb District of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: First of all, in -- yes, if we could go back a little bit, just a few clips, to show the person who had just spoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, anyway, General Vasiljevic, we heard a person say: "You know that we are under the command of the Territorial Defence of the Serbian District of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem." Here we have his image on the screen. Who is this?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: That is Arkan Raznjatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what Arkan stated to the interviewer, was that consistent with information that the Security Administration had in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You also mention in paragraph 76 of your statement that several members of the Serbian Volunteer Guard had criminal records.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could play the next clip, which is page 2 of the English transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "I remember when Arkan led me through the dormitories and one of them he said there are over 250 years of prison time in this room."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: General, who was speaking just then?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: That is the so-called Captain Dragan Vasiljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what he says about the criminal histories of members of Arkan's unit, was that consistent with information that you had in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: When we collected intelligence about who Arkan was, he had his first group that consisted of about 20 persons. I think that they took their oath at the Pokajnica church. We checked the names that we had, and these were persons who had, according to the information that we had then, 102 years of prison time. Obviously since Captain Dragan was in a bigger dormitory, it turned out to be over 200 years of prison time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: General, in paragraph 77 of your statement you describe seeing General Biorcevic, commander of the Novi Sad Corps, on television praising Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I would like to start the next video-clip at 52 minutes and 4 seconds. This is page 4 of the English transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "... encirclements and in smaller enclaves Mr. Arkan, the commander of the Serbian Volunteer Guard, acted very neatly, wisely and in a planed fashion. "Narrator: Certain generals understood the message. Among them, the first was the commander of the Novi Sad Corps, Andrija Biorcevic. "General Biorcevic: What Arkan told you, whom I consider a just and honourable Serb, he was rich even before the war. In this war, he had lost more than he had gained. Where is your wound? Show it. Serbian hero. Look at his finger. Which one is it? See what it looks like. I tell him, Go and have it treated. And he replies, I'm with you."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: General, who was -- can you confirm who was speaking on the stage during the clip?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: That was General Biorcevic, commander of the Novi Sad Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how was what he was saying during this segment compared to what your yourself had heard General Biorcevic state?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what he said speaks most tellingly of what General Biorcevic was like himself. He glorifies Arkan and practically he was never his subordinate directly. Maybe he did carry out operations in the area of his operations group. I mean, the way in which he spoke speaks tellingly and sufficiently about him himself. As far as I can see, he is a lieutenant-colonel general at the time, so that may be after the Vukovar operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we can look at one more segment which is going to begin at 58 minutes and 35 seconds. Before the break, you were mentioning Arkan and his units' involvement in smuggling.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can play this clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this is page 6 of the English transcript. Perhaps we could go back and start it again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Each time the Serb Volunteer Guard returned from Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina, apart from APCs and tanks there was also a large number of container lorries in the column and that was their characteristic. It had to do with looting."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: General who was just speaking there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: This was General Milovanovic, who was Chief of Staff for General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And with regard to what General Milovanovic stated with regard to the looting activities of Arkan in the RSK and RS, how did that compare with information that the Security Administration had in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the papers that we had the opportunity of seeing earlier on, well, that is absolutely correct. Because of this awareness of looting and taking this property out of the Krajina in 1992, I think it was my second visit in Vukovar, I noticed that there were these units that were stealing. We ordered that check-points be placed on the periphery of the Krajina and when I returned at the toll point near Belgrade, lots of stolen goods had already been taken out and everybody was taking it all over the place. However, when these check-points were placed on the exits out of the Krajina, Arkan was not prevented in doing what he wanted to do because he took certain byways and managed to get out with this stolen property. So he did have this image of constant looting in the theatre of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, may these series of video-clips be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That is under -- under one number, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. We combined all those clips into one -- one -- one document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2916, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: General, in paragraph 134 of your statement, you discuss the Leva Supoderica and the Petrova Gora detachments which were operating in Vukovar in 1991. Can you tell us, to whom were these two detachments subordinate?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: They were subordinate to the staff of the Territorial Defence in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: At some time, were they -- at some point in time, were they resubordinated?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. During some combat operations, they were resubordinated, practically to Operations Group South, or specifically to Assault Detachment 1 in General Mrksic's order for attack. He was commander of Operations Group South.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if you know, for how long were they resubordinated to Operations Group South?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: He were -- they were resubordinated during the operations that were taking place. Apart from those operations, practically they were not under the command of the operation group, so while combat operations were underway and within the tasks issued through this order. Afterwards, they would return to their original unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: When these detachments were not participating in a combat operation, to whom did they report?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether they reported to anyone, but it was the staff of the Territorial Defence that had jurisdiction over them. They admitted them as one of their units.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In paragraph 134 of your statement, you mentioned that some members of these units, or the volunteer units operating in Vukovar, were committing crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could look at 65 ter 532. This is tab 88.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what we have in front of us is a periodical operations report of the OB Guards Motorised Brigade to the SSNO Security Administration. And if we can scroll up a bit, we can see that it's dated 7 November 1992. And if we could go to the bottom of -- of the page in the original. And page 2 of the English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think the year is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's -- thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Yes, the date is 7 November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we can look at the bottom page of the original and page 2 of -- of the English version, the report states: "With regards the Vukovar operation, the Serbian nationalistic and the Chetnik propaganda are taking on a serious dimension which, in its breadth, outstrips by far the results in combat of the volunteer groups and the members of the paramilitary units. The nationalistic and ideological symbols, nationalistic songs, the speeches of Vojislav Seselj, the liquidation of POWs by Chetniks, et cetera, are all unjustifiably tolerated." Given the date of this document, 7 November 1991, who -- who had the responsibility to investigate these liquidations and, for that matter, any other crimes committed by these groups?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I have already explained that if these were crimes that belonged to the jurisdiction of the military courts, then the procedure was supposed to be carried out by the military organs. Otherwise, if the crimes committed did not fall under this chapter then it was the civilian organs in the territory that were in charge. Everyone who had information about such things takes place was supposed to make the authorities aware of what was happening so that proceedings could be initiated. So this is information that was sent to the chief of security in the office of the federal secretary for national defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I understand that this document is -- is pending admission into evidence, so I won't tender it at this time. If we could have on -- on the screen, 65 ter 680. This is tab 110.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: General, what we have in front of us is a pass dated 22 November 1991. And if we look at the upper right-hand corner of the document, we see reference to the -- I'm sorry, the upper left-hand corner, we see reference to the Vukovar Municipal Territorial Defence Staff. First of all, before which get into this document, could you tell us just generally what was the purpose and role of a TO Staff?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: TO Staffs in the territory of Western Slavonia had under their jurisdiction local units of the Territorial Defence. So they had a command function in respect of these units in the area of their responsibility. So practically, to simplify matters, these were military commands that had subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And in the SBWS, who appointed the TO Staffs?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I could say what the regulation said. At the beginning of my testimony, I said that the appointment of the commander of territorial staff of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem was supposed to be verified by a final decision of the Presidency of the SFRY. However, as far as I know, that was never done. Now who appointed these staffs here? It could have been the government of the the SAO Krajina, Western Srem, that territory. I've already explained that an important influence over everything that happened there was exercised by Radovan Stojicic, Badza, with his command post in Dalj.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn now to this -- this document, this pass that was issued on the 22nd of November, 1991. Could you tell us, what does this document indicate to you with regard to the command and control over the Leva Supoderica detachment?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: On this document, one cannot see that it is just Milan Lancuzanin. Down there it says that someone signed on his behalf. He was either absent at that moment or perhaps he transferred this authority that somebody could sign on his behalf. However it clearly states "commander of the detachment," and we know that it is Leva Supoderica, and it says Milan Lancuzanin. Now, within the framework of what I said previously, up here we see that this detachment belongs to the Serb District of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem and that this is the municipal staff of the TO in Vukovar. That is confirmation of who these units on the ground were subordinated to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And do you know by 22 November 1991, were there any combat operations ongoing in Vukovar itself?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, that was over.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see at the bottom of this document a stamp. Can you tell us what kind of stamp that is?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: It's a military stamp. It's the stamp of military post 4795. That is the military post code of the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you explain why a -- a JNA stamp would it be affixed to a SBWS TO document?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I can make an assumption. They don't have stamps of their own, when speaking of the Territorial Defence. Before this 22nd of November, he was within that operations group of the 1st Assault Group of the Operations Group South. Operations were over. That's the 22nd of November. They are releasing some of these persons. And now these persons are returning their weapons. That is to say, they're being dismissed from the units and they're returning their weapons. Probably the weapons were received from this military post. And then that is confirmed by these signatures here. If I can read this, it says major - and I don't know whether it's a person by the name of Nikola - he actually confirms that this rifle number such and such was received. So this stamp was not used to confirm the right of this Djordje to leave the Leva Supoderica Unit. Rather, that is a confirmation of him receiving this rifle that the Guards Brigade had issued him with.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2319, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In paragraph 144 of your statement you describe a report that you received from Major Sljivancanin after the fall of Vukovar which you found to be dissatisfactory.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have P2001.1981 on e-court. This is tab 114.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this is a report from the security organ of the Guards Motorised Brigade to the SSNO Security Administration, dated 10 December 1991. And if we could turn to the last page. We can see that it is signed by Lieutenant-Colonel Sljivancanin. General, do you recognise this report?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's a report which I requested from Lieutenant-Colonel Sljivancanin after the cessation of hostilities in Vukovar. I wanted a report about the activities of the security organ during the Vukovar operation. This is the report he drafted and that is why Sljivancanin submits it directly to the Security Administration rather than to the chief of his section. Probably he did provide a copy to Lieutenant-Colonel Dragan Djukic who was chief of his sector. I criticise him in my statement too because he didn't deal with the key counter-intelligence tasks. He mostly speaks about the combat in Vukovar and points out some problems with the -- that they had with the paramilitary units and the TO. I was not content with this report. I replied to him that he had not given an account of counter-intelligence activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 2 of this document. And towards the bottom, at least of the English version, maybe it's more towards the middle of the original version, Sljivancanin reports: "The government of the SO of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem are mostly to blame for this kind of behaviour and poor response. This government appointed Territorial Defence Staff commanders who are neither generally respected or valued by the people owing to their previous services as well as appointing to high positions people who were corrupt and tried and tested in dirty business and activities." Is what Lieutenant-Colonel Sljivancanin is reporting here, is that consistent with information that the Security Administration had?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: General, after the fall of Vukovar, what sort of crimes were members of volunteer groups committing in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: There was some quantity of information from the organs in the field. I'm speaking about looting houses, the killing of individuals who were characterises as Ustasha. That's what they called them. Then Croats who would not heave Vukovar were persecuted, and these are mostly the crimes I'm talking about. I would like to add that TO units at that time were not subordinated to the army because there were no more combat activities in Vukovar. And that's what Sljivancanin writes about.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 937 on e-court. This is tab 119.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What we have in front of us is a report on clearing up the battle-field ground and restoring Vukovar and other endangered sectors from the 1st Military District Command to the SSNO Operations Administration for Logistics, and the date of the document is 20 February 1992. If we could turn to page 12 of the original, page 19 of the English. And if I can draw your attention to item (C), it reports: "In December and January, the commission conducting clearance located and identified fresh human bodies. This means that the clandestine liquidation of people was being carried out in the town, with atrocities being committed (slaughtering, burning, gun-shots to the temple, homicide by using big-game hunting rifles, and other crimes)." It then states that the security organs undertook immediate measures to protect the population. General are you aware of what measures, if any, were taken?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot name any specific measures, but one of them was that the security organs reported about individual killings to the security organ of the 1st Military District and so on. Of the measures taken, which started after the end of combat activities in Vukovar, which means on the 21st or 22nd of November, I drafted a report to the highest military commanders, General Kadijevic and his assistants, about looting, killings, expulsions of persons from their homes, and so on. On the 27th of November, he ordered that an order be issued about clearing up in all the zones where military units were present. A result of that was an order of the Presidency of the SFRY, dated the 10th of December, 1991 about removing all paramilitaries and there was a provision that in case any armed units were to remain there, which conditions they had to comply with. This started happening around the 21st in the area of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You referenced the 21st. Is that the 21st of December?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I mentioned that after the 21st of November, and if I said December, I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You didn't misspeak. It simply wasn't clear to me on the record, so I just wanted to clarify that. Did you have a conversation with the head of the 1st Military District security organ, General Mile Babic, about paramilitary crimes after the fall of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. As far as I remember now, on the 4th of December, I went to the Novi Sad Corps' security organ. I saw General Milic Jovanovic [phoen]. They were also active on the ground. I was briefed about counter-intelligence matters, and he passed on his information about the events on the ground. He mentioned killings, persecution, and crimes committed in his zone. I had not received such information from the chief of security of the 1st Military District, although he had sent that information along regular lines. When I returned to Belgrade, I went to see General Babic and was briefed about the usual procedure concerning counter-intelligence matters, and I also mentioned that I had information from the 24th Corps which information never reached our administration. And then he replied that they mostly were taking measures at the local level and obviously he didn't consider it necessary to write to the Security Administration about such information that was not about counter-intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you find such a response by General Babic to be satisfactory?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Because it was his duty to forward the information received from the security organs at corps level, although they do not strictly belong to the jurisdiction of the security organs; that is, killings, and looting, and so on. Because there is a list of things that are part of a jurisdiction. However, these were important events that, first of all, the commanders should be informed about so that they can pass such information on. They can ask that a prosecutor become active. And on the 20th of October, 1991, I got the first information from him about the events at Lovas. I wasn't satisfied with the description of that event. The information was incomplete. And then I asked for additional information, only then was I able to draft a report for the SSNO and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned at this meeting with the 12th Corps on the 4th of December that you were informed about a number of killings and persecutions. Can you recall where those killings had taken place? Do you recall the locations?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: These were the villages of Sotin and Antin. These were the most characteristic locations because the most people had been killed there; 19, 20, 21, persons, and the modus operandi was typical. The security organs on the ground at corps level informed the local organs of the MUP. They conducted an online --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: On-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The name of the person involved was Zavicic, I believe, and they initiated the procedure to identify the perpetrators. It didn't -- it wasn't limited to the description of the events. And later on, the civilian organs did what they did and I don't know how it ended. But our information came directly from the field, and that can be seen from the previous document that he showed, the analysis that was made for the organs of the MUP of Serbia. They were always informed and somebody always conducted an on-site investigation and the initial activities, as required.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned that around 19 to 21 persons were killed. What -- what were their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: There were both Croats and Hungarians. According to the initial information compiled by the security organs, that was preceded by placing labels on their houses, saying that within 24 hours they had to leave the village otherwise they would be removed by force. The ones who did not leave were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall whether the perpetrators of these crimes were known?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: According to the information the security organs were collecting, they came up with a name, and they informed the on-site investigation team of that. One person was suspected of having participated in that. If I'm not mistaken, his last name was Gogic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Paragraph 171 of your statement, you discuss how Vesna Bosanac was falsely accused of committing atrocities against Serbs who were at the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could look at page 11 of the original and page 18 of the English. If I could draw your attention to item (B). If we could scroll over a little bit in the original so I can make sure we have the right one in front of us. Scroll -- scroll over to -- to the left. Yes. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we look under item (B) it is reported that: "The case of the burning of bodies in the incinerator of Vukovar Hospital and transplants of body parts was shown to be completely unfounded. This report was the product of certain organs of ... SAO ... Krajina, certain physicians from Vukovar Hospital, and part of the local unobjective press." How does that finding compare to the information obtained by the security organs of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: The operative team of the security organs at Sremska Mitrovica, and, among other things, they interviewed Vesna Bosanac, never mentioned such allegations. Before she could be exchanged, she was interrogated by an investigative magistrate of the Belgrade military court. They also had at their disposal materials compiled by the operative team at Sremska Mitrovica and they concluded that there was no foundation that she committed such crimes and allowed her exchange. What you have just read out is an authentic reproduction of what the sanitation commission for the battle-field had stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2918, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And related to this last issue that you have just testified about, if we could have 65 ter 969 on the screen. This is tab 120. This is an article from the "Novosti" periodical, entitled: "Vesna Bosanac, Dr. Mengele, dated 6 March 1992." You had an opportunity to review this article -- we could zoom in a little bit for him. You had an opportunity to review this article during proofing. How did the allegations against Ms. Bosanac in this article compared to what you were reading in the press at the time.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I haven't now read the details of this article. I see that this was published on the 4th of March, 1992, in "Vecernji Novosti." At that time criminal proceedings were underway against me before the military court, and one -- one of the charges was that I protected war criminals and had them released. There were several such articles in "Politika" and "Vecernje Novosti." They were about this Dr. Mengele who had cut body parts off Serbian prisoners of war, and so on, and other nonsense. It is clear that no amputations were ever made. In hospital safes, there were only such limbs that were affected by gangrene. And at Vukovar Hospital there were also four JNA members taken prisoner. One of them was Corporal Sasa Petrovic, I think, and he a foot wound, because he stepped on an anti-personnel mine. He was treated correctly and fairly and remained in active service in the Army of Yugoslavia for a while subsequently. And the other soldiers were also well treated medically.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2919, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: General, I want to return to the issue of TO and volunteer units operating in Vukovar after its fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have on e-court document P151. This is tab 215.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this is a decision of the SBWS government dated 21 January 1992. And if I may draw your attention to the -- the very first paragraph. It states that this discussion was issued at the proposal of Colonel Ratko Ristic, assistant commander of the Novi Sad Corps for civilian affairs. And if we look under item 1, the decision authorises the 1st Military District to disband the unit led by Kameni stationed in Vukovar, and under item 2 states that the 1st Military District Command may issue an order for the implementation of item 1 after agreement with the SBWS Ministry of Interior regarding the engagement of police forces of the Vukovar SUP for the joint accomplishment of this task. General, does this decision indicate anything to you with regard to the relationship between the JNA and Kameni's unit after the fall of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I will probably have to give a lengthy introduction what this has to do with. This has to do with an order about the disbanding of paramilitary units. It's an order of the 10th of December. That was preceded by an order by General Kadijevic on the 27th of November -- November. In that order by the commander of the 1st Military District, it is specified what should happen with these territorial units, and the unit of Miodrag Lancuzanin had to -- was supposed to join the 24th Novi Sad Corps. However, they didn't join that corps. They remained behind in the territory. So volunteers and other territorial units were still roaming the territory, and they did not subordinate to the JNA, as was required by the regulations, and Arkan's unit was one of them. General Zivota Panic ordered the security organ, Colonel Petkovic, on the 28th of January, that he should see Radovan Stojicic, Badza, and order him to remove Arkan's units from the terrain. This is very telling about Stojicic's influence. He said that he would carry out the order but that they were planning to establish some sort of brigade of their own. Since Lancuzanin, with his units, was not part of the 24th Corps but stay -- stayed behind in that territory, and all the units had to be removed because of the crimes they had been -- that had been committed, what now follows is a funny -- is some funny language. The government of the SAO allows the 1st Military District to remove Kameni because he had become a nuisance. It would be logical to submit a request to General Panic to do the job in the field considering everything that is contained in various reports and Sljivancanin's report about what was happening, who was really commanding and who was supposed to command but didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm sorry, General, we might have missed the end of your answer there.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The transcript reads: "... Sljivancanin's report about what was happening, who was really commanding and who was supposed to command but didn't." Is that the end of your sentence?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Who was really supposed to -- who was supposed to command but didn't. And the other way around: Who didn't command but was supposed to. That was how I ended my sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. If these armed elements, Arkan's unit, the -- the Leva Supoderica Unit under Kameni, if they were, in fact, subordinated to the JNA, would General Panic have had to go through the SBWS government and Badza to seek to remove these groups?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to put it very briefly and perhaps this is an unusual way of speaking before this Court. Heaven for bid that the commander ask some self-styled president, self-styled districts to ask for approval what the military is going to do in relation to their own authority, well, that's why I'm saying that this formation was supposed to be put this way. It is not that it is being -- that they are being allowed to do it but they should just ask if they would do it since they were not capable of doing it themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
