utterances.text: All right. Towards the beginning of your testimony, you had made reference to the Velepromet detention facility, and I would like to show you a document, which is 65 ter 553. This is tab 90. This is a Guards Brigade security organ report to the security organ of the office of the SSNO dated 9 November -- 9 November 1991. And if we could turn to page 2 of this document, and if we could look at the penultimate paragraph, this report states: "Over 300 persons have been evacuated to Velepromet where they are being individually processed. During the day, around 100 persons were processed, of which around 25 have been selected; they are of interest to the security organs in the further collection of information about Ustasha positions and forces and in possible exchanges for captured JNA members." And then if we look at the final paragraph, it is written: "These persons are currently in Velepromet." We can account for the 25 persons that were identified by the security organs. What does this tell us about the 275 persons who were not identified by the security organs, as of security interest?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: This is one of the fairly rare reports of the security organ of the Guards Brigade that had to do with their actual tasks and purview. This is a report concerning a segment of counter-intelligence. I think that earlier on we talked about detainees, prisoners, and they selected 25 who were of interest. And it says here why they are of interest. And there's also some other information about connections that some persons had with the HDZ and so on. So this is a counter-intelligence report. As far as I can see, it was compiled by Mladen Karan again, the assistant commander for counter-intelligence. Now you asked me what about the remaining 300 persons. There is no answer. It is only natural that they would have remained at the collection centre at Velepromet. I think his name is Ljubinko. Maybe I will make a mistake about his last name. I think it was Stojanovic. The staff of TO Vukovar had their own person in charge of selection, security processing of persons who were detained at Velepromet. These persons, these 25, to the best of my knowledge from Captain First Class Borisavljevic, who was the security officer at the Vukovar barracks, they were transferred to the barracks and then interviews continued with them. Information -- more in-depth information was sought, and so on. During the next stage, I think that they were released, as I've already said, and were sent to Begejci, the collection centre there. As for these person, I cannot say because no one reported to me about that when I came to Vukovar and I'm not aware of their fate. Maybe somebody from Slavonia could give an answer. However, we do know what happened in Velepromet. However, that is what happened in relation to the 19th, 20th, that is what I have to say about the type of collection centre that that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2920, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: As OG South commander, who was Colonel Mrksic's superior?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: There are two situations that we can look at, and then there are two different persons that are immediate superiors to him. In peacetime, his immediate superior is the Chef de cabinet of the minister federal secretary for national defence, General Vuk Obradovic. Within combat operations when he was sent to Vukovar he was subordinated to the commander of the 1st Military District, General Zivota Panic. After those operations, he returned to the office at the SSNO and was under them again.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: While Colonel Mrksic was reporting or under the command of -- of -- of General Panic, did he continue to provide information to Obradovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but I can assume that information was sent to Obradovic because from the federal secretary's office and Vuk Obradovic's office, then Colonel Nebojsa Pavkovic was there too. He was sent to General Mrksic, to the brigade command, as a person who could in a way help by way of giving professional advice, et cetera. However, he was not subordinated to Zivota Panic. Along the vertical chain he was linked to Vuk Obradovic, so I assume that if not regularly they did inform Vuk Obradovic every day about what happened and what kind of problems there were, like one of the problems listed here, that 26 soldiers who were Croats who were within the brigade asked how their status would be resolved later because they don't want to desert from the JNA. They request to know how they're going to leave the JNA and how they're going to go back to that setting. So that had to do with the internal problems with that brigade, and Pavkovic probably had daily communication about that with Obradovic, and vice versa. Now Mrksic, apart from that, whether he communicated, I can just make an assumption, but I do not have any specific knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In paragraphs 165 to 172 of your statement, you address the collection centres that were established in Serbia for a persons captured during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 6459 on e-court. This is tab 209.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a 1st Military District order dated 15 September 1991. And if we look at the first paragraph it reads: "Pursuant to the SSNO order of 14 September 1991, with the aim of examining, identifying, settling securing and regulating the status-related issues of the persons captured in the inter-ethnic conflicts in the territory of the Republic of Croatia, I hereby issue the following ..." Could you give us some insights? What was the SSNO order that was issued on the 14th of September?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: It is clear what the order is. It is probably the BB that is unclear, and that means without a number, "bez broje," that is to say that this is an oral order of General Kadijevic issued on the 14th of September, 1991, to resolved the question of taking in prisoners of war, refugees, from the combat zone. That is to say, the establishment of collection centres of the JNA. On the basis of this oral order he issued on the 14th of September, I can say that he then ordered the start of the Vukovar operation too, that started, because all-out attacks by Croatian paramilitary forces against all JNA barracks started on the 15th. On the basis of this order, General Blagoje Adzic issued his order that he sent to the commanders of the Military Districts, the 1st, 2nd, 3rd Military District, so not only the first one. And on the basis of that order of General Blagoje Adzic, I don't know whether you have it, but I think that I know the number 5-86, if I'm not mistaken. I know that by heart. Commanders of Military Districts then regulated the establishment of collection centres, their organisation, their tasks, et cetera. And this is one of the orders of the commander of the 1st Military District to the assistant commander for logistics because this was within his domain to set up a commission for identification and everything else that is done in collection centres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I have two more questions and then I'm done with this document, if I could just go one more minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just very quickly, General, prior to this 14 September 1991 order, were there any JNA-operated collection centres for persons captured during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And very quickly, what was the first collection centre that was established as a result of this order?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of this order, the collection centre of Begejci was established on the basis of the order issued by the commander of the 1st Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what date was that that the collection centre was established?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: The order is dated the 16th of September. That is to say, when he received this order, that is, the 15th, so then from the 16th. That was the order to establish the collection centre in Begejci and that the command of the Novi Sad Corps is in charge of this with regard to all matters, that they should appoint their own commander of this centre, and also a unit that will provide security for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2921, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, we're moving on to a new topic, so we can break here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: General Vasiljevic, this is the time - a little bit over even - for our second break. We'll take 30 minutes, or 32 even, and come back at 12.50. The Court Usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: General, I want to briefly return to the topic of the paramilitary groups who were operating in the SBWS in late 1991 and early 1992. Return to a question that I asked that I'm not sure I got a clear answer, and perhaps I can phrase it differently. You've testified - and it's in your statement - that on the 28th of January, General Panic ordered Colonel Petkovic to tell Badza to remove Arkan's unit from the area. And we also looked at a SBWS decision which states that Colonel Ristic requested the SBWS government to take certain actions with regard to Kameni's unit. My question to you is: If Arkan's unit and if Kameni's unit were subordinate to the JNA, what actions would General Panic have taken with regard to those units?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, had they been subordinate to the JNA, he would have directly either disarmed those units or kept them within the JNA under the conditions that had been prescribed by the Presidency on the 10th of December, 1991. So he would fully be in charge of either expelling and disarming these units or admitting them within his own ranks if they so wished and if they met the requirements specified in the order of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Would he have gone through Badza or the SBWS government to accomplish that, if they were subordinated to him?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: If they were subordinated to him, then he asks those that they are subordinated to, to expel them and to act in accordance with the order of the Presidency, or to remind them of the order of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And was Badza subordinated to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: To who?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, was Badza, was he reporting directly to General Panic? Was he a subordinate of General Panic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I know that he was not subordinated to General Panic. Now whether he submitted reports to him, if he had asked for that, I don't know. But he was not subordinated to General Zivota Panic, although he did come to some meetings that were held by Panic. Mr. Goran Hadzic attended these meetings from time to time, but he was not subordinate to General Panic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you testified that General Panic ordered Colonel Petkovic to instruct Badza to remove Arkan's unit. Was Colonel Petkovic in a position to order Badza to do anything?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I would like to change topics now. Now, in paragraph 168 of your statement, you mentioned that the "Politika" newspaper reported that Goran Hadzic announced a SBWS government decision that all Croat prisoners from Vukovar be handed over to them. And this is after the fall of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 644 on e-court. This is tab 102.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a "Politika" article dated 21 November 1991. And if we could zoom in to the left-hand column. And just for the record, this article is entitled: "The most hardened will be tried in Vukovar." And if we look at the second paragraph, Goran Hadzic is reported as stating: "The government of the Serbian district met in session for the first time today in liberated Vukovar and the only item on the agenda of the session was the question of how the most hardened criminals were to be handled." And further on, Mr. Hadzic is reported as asserting that the judiciary of Serbia and the federal judiciary only have jurisdiction in the second-instance and third-instance proceedings against criminals from Vukovar. First of all, how does what is reported in this article compared to what you recall reading and viewing in the press around this time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in this context there was constant insistence upon them having their own judiciary organs and that they were in charge of the fate or trials of war criminals, as they call them here, but actually these are prisoners. Several times, as for persons that were in collection centres, they made many efforts to have them under their control. It is interesting here that it says that their organs are in charge. In first instances and second instances would be the Republic of Serbia, its organs; and then, third instance be would the Supreme Court of the Republic of Serbia. However, they were not a constituent part of the SFRY at the time, that is number one. Number two, secondly, we know, unfortunately, what their judgement was when they had an opportunity to pass one. I see the date here, and that's only a day's difference from Ovcara. And therefore, this insistence, and that was also in contact with Colonel Maksimovic, when they visited on the 10th of December and in their contacts with me three days later on 13th December, in Mitrovica, the same efforts were being made. That they should take over, that they are in charge, that they spilt their blood, that they know who criminals are, and so on, and that they have to try them. So let me not go outside this context. If necessary, they would ensure that even by arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we look further down, we see that Mr. Hadzic is reported as thanking the Serbian government. What is the significance of that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't see the article. Perhaps you could explain. It will be easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yeah. Yes, I'll just actually read it because it is a little difficult to read in the original version. It says: "This time, Goran Hadzic said, on behalf of all Serbs in this autonomous district, I wish to express our deepest appreciation for how Serbia has treated us. I wish to thank the Serbian government, Assembly and all Serbian citizens for their generous aid in this horrendous struggle." General, what do you see as the significance of him thanking the Serbian government?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to -- wouldn't like to speak about the significance. But why is he thanking them? It's a fact that the Serbian government, as he said, provided generous assistance during the whole period of constituting the government of Slavonia and Srem and throughout its existence. It went from funds, through weapons, to sending people from Serbia to the territory to assist that government, starting from Radovan Stojicic, Badza, to others. There were also people from the top echelons of the state security of Serbia. And now he is taking the opportunity to express his gratitude in a ceremonious fashion. And, frankly, speaking, he had good reason to be grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this article be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2922, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: General, in paragraph 169 of your statement, you describe your meeting with Goran Hadzic at Sremska Mitrovica KP Dom. And at the beginning of your testimony here today, you've clarified the date of that meeting as the 13th of December, 1991, rather than the 10th of December, 1991. However, you also testified that on the 10th of December, that persons from the SAO were also at the KP Dom. Can you tell us, first of all, how did you learn about this visit on the 10th of December?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: When I reviewed my notes, I found out that on the 10th of December, I was neither in Belgrade nor in Mitrovica. I was in Zagreb for exchanges. And then I remembered that there was a visit and that they were in contact with Colonel Jugoslav Maksimovic. That's who they talked to. In "Vecernje Novosti" they published an article about Goran Hadzic threatening Vasiljevic; namely, that I would be held accountable for releasing war criminals. And that's how we learned that such a meeting really had taken place. I took a look at some material from the archives and I found a note drafted by Colonel Jugoslav Maksimovic about that visit. I would also like to mention that he signed that as head of the operative team of the security organ and not as is sometimes stated in some other -- in some other sources that he was commander of the collection centre. He was not. What did he write there? That Goran Hadzic had come, and Mr. Susa, minister of the justice, then the minister of the interior, Mr. Bogunovic and another person who remains unidentified. He states that from the very beginning, they had -- they were very arrogant. They were insulted by the fact that Vesna Bosanac had been exchanged. And by the fact that war criminals were being released and that people were being released from collection centres at all without them being asked about it, and they had taken prisoner all these people and they had shed their own blood to capture all these Ustashas and so on. Susa was the loudest. Hadzic mostly kept quiet. He only mentioned when he was leaving the room, You'll be left without a general. They wanted to be able to take part in operative -- the operative processing of the detainees and they wanted to -- they wanted the results of this operative processing. Likewise, since they had their own judicial organs they wanted to be in charge of what would happen to those detainees. Whatever they said to Maksimovic was also mentioned in a letter of theirs in which they contacted first General Zivota Panic, but he didn't reply, and then they sent that letter to the SSNO. They also wrote to Maksimovic that they know -- that they knew who he was because in the first wave when people were pulled out of Vukovar, he, with the Red Cross, wanted -- or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Had 1500 Ustashas as they said, actually, 1500 Croats, leave the place because they wanted to go to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were at Sremska Mitrovica in the Red Cross facility and they objected to these Ustashas being transported out of Vukovar. That's what they called all Croats. And they also commented that they knew who was -- who bore most of blame for all that, and that's why we would be left without a general. That was a threat. Maksimovic was in contact the people at the collection centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me just go briefly back to some of the things you've just stated. First of all, you mentioned that at this 10 December meeting, the minister of the interior was also present. Can you repeat his last name?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Bogunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you mentioned that one of things that was stated to Maksimovic is that you would be left without a general. How did you interpret that? Who were they referring to?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: There's nothing to interpret. On that day, I took the first group to Zagreb to be exchanged for members of the security organ taken prisoner in Croatia and some other prisoners. These were from the Gospic garrison. On the 10th, they came to Mitrovica to react because the media had already published the news that Vesna Bosanac had been released and that the exchange -- that I was in -- in charge of the exchange. And they were reacting to that. Why had it been done, why had they not been asked that these people were criminals. And Maksimovic said, No, we're -- we won't let our general -- we'll back up our general, in other words. And that general, that was me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Prior to your meeting with Mr. Hadzic and his delegation on the 13th of December, did you have a conversation with Colonel Maksimovic regarding the 10 December meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No. He was at Sremska Mitrovica. His letter was sent to the person in charge in the Security Administration. I wasn't in the field much, or in meetings. To us, this was an insignificant event. It was part of their efforts to -- to get these prisoners, to be in charge of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, finally, just to clarify, in your statement, you make reference to a newspaper article published later in 1992. And this is 65 ter Exhibit 772, tab 32, which describes a meeting between Mr. Hadzic and his delegation and Colonel Maksimovic. Which meeting is that referring to, that newspaper article? And we see it on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, there's no date here. I don't know when the article was published. Maybe further down I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: General, and you don't need really to look too much into this article because it's in your statement, and this is the article that you provided to the Tribunal. And my question is simply whether this article relates to the 10 December meeting or the 13 December meeting.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No, this article refers -- refers to the 10 December meeting. At the time when it was published, I didn't see it. I didn't have the opportunity to read it then. I only got it on the -- in 1998, when my brother died, and I took over some of his things, he collected such clippings, and that's when I first saw it. It was -- it was about Hadzic accusing Vasiljevic when he went to see Colonel Maksimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to now turn just briefly to the 13 December meeting, which you do describe in a fair amount of detail in your statement. But can you tell us, how did it come about that this meeting happened on the 13th of December?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that the meeting had been called and that there would be a meeting with Mr. Hadzic and the other persons. On the 13th of December, as I said, I was in a meeting with the military prosecutor and the operative team of the security organ where there was talk about professional problems in connection with the documentation of the activities they had initiated. At that meeting with the military prosecutor which took place in the -- in the correctional and penal facility that is in the administration rooms that I didn't know that this meeting was taking place elsewhere. I don't know whether later they came to Mitrovica or not but it doesn't matter really. The same persons came, Goran Hadzic, Vojin Susa, Minister Bogunovic. I don't remember a fourth person, but there may have been one. During that conversation, which was different from the one with Jugoslav Maksimovic, they were not as arrogant as then. Secondly, I didn't know then that they had come to Maksimovic two days earlier. I only had some rough indication that they had been there before. I was in contact with them, but it was a short meeting and it was not tense. There were complaints about war criminals being released. They considered those their own prisoners and they repeated those phrases that they shed their blood to catch them, and you're releasing them without asking anybody, and we want you to stop this practice, and that -- that they had to be consulted about everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me stop you there because much of this is in your statement, so we don't need to repeat it here on the record. But, can you tell us was the JNA, in fact, releasing war criminals?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No. Whatever the operative team of the security organ had found out, discovered and documented, a great number of people were released to go where they wanted to. They were not exchanged. This was done by the mediation of the Red Cross. Those who were suspected of having committed crime, mostly armed rebellion, that is, those who were members of armed formations in Croatia who had attacked the JNA, were not released. If the crimes committed were less serious such as merely being a member of a paramilitary formation in Croatia they were exchanged for JNA members taken prisoner. That would be another category, to call it that. Whereas, those who were suspected of committing serious crimes, such as war crimes, were not exchanged. Charges were pressed against them with the military court in Belgrade. As far as I remember, there were 182 such persons against whom criminal proceedings were launched. They couldn't be exchanged, and they were under the jurisdiction of the military court. Investigations were conducted and about 80 persons were tried and there were first-instance judgements in 25 cases. And later on, there was a -- an all-for-all exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You also mentioned -- mention in your statement that you suggested to the SBWS delegation that they could help the JNA by providing any information they had about crimes committed by the prisoners in the Vukovar area, that they could provide that information to your security organs. How did they react to that suggestion?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: There were no special reactions, such as, No, we don't want to do that. They requested to be directly involved in these talks. It was our position, not only mine but that of the military organs, that they cannot interfere with the activities of military security and military -- the military judiciary. That's what Colonel Maksimovic also had told them: You cannot be involved in any talks. If you have any useful information, give it to us, and we will use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did the SBWS organs ever provide any information to the JNA security organisations, regarding the prisoners at these collection centres?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No. They were supposed to give such information to the Security Administration or the -- our security organ of the 1st Military District, but I never got anything like that and I don't believe that they provide any.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to switch topics. But before I do, General, though I haven't received a notification from the interpreters, I think it will be helpful if you slow down a little bit for them so they can be sure to catch everything you are saying and make sure it's on the record, and also I would remind you again to focus on my question so I can get through this material. In paragraphs 147 to 153 of your statement you describe the information you received about the crimes committed in Lovas and in particular the killing of a number of local Croats by the Dusan Silni detachment. And in paragraph 151 of your statement, and I think you mentioned it earlier today, that a criminal report was filed against certain members of the Serbian TO who may have been linked with that crime and that that was filed with the military prosecutor's office. Can you tell us, do you know what happened to that case?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I filed the criminal report about the case at Lovas. It was a criminal report against four TO members from the Valjevo detachment, and there were also other persons who had taken part in that. What later happened to that and how it all ended, I don't know, because I retired relatively fast, but I was also very busy with paramilitaries in other areas. I know that four military persons were -- were processed, or, rather, that proceedings were launched against them. I don't know what happened to the eight from Dusan Silni, but certainly the organs in charge were informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 80 of your statement you identify Ljuban Devetak as commander of the Dusan Silni and you also name several of the members of Dusan Silni that provided security for Devetak, including Nikola Vukovic and Ljubodrag Jelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could please look at 65 ter 3670. This is tab 204. And if we could turn to page 7 in the both the English and the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see that this is a 5 December certificate confirming that Ljubodrag Jelic has been a member of the Lovas TO as a volunteer territorial from 8 October 1991. And if we could now go to page 10, this is a 10 January 1992 certificate confirming that Nikola Vukovic has been a member of the Lovas TO as a volunteer territorial who participated in the liberation of villages in war operations from 10 October 1991 to 10 January 1992. General, what do these documents indicate to you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: This document confirms what we have already discussed and what I talked about. There was a Lovas TO Staff, and they were issuing certificates to members of paramilitary units who - these two specifically - took part in the event of the 17th or 18th of October, when civilians were driven into a minefield. This -- these certificates are -- were issued to them in January 1992. They should have been tried and serving their sentence at that time, but they were still at large, out in the field, and these certificates are routine certificates that were issued by the TO to such persons and others for them to be able to exercise some rights because they had taken part in war, and their commander was Ljuban Devetak.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this series of documents be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2923, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: General, I'd like to shift to another topic. Could you tell us, at any time in 1991 or 1992 in the SBWS region did the JNA consider itself an occupation -- an army of occupation under the laws of war?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No. The JNA was active in a territory of the country to which it belonged, and that was Yugoslavia. An army cannot occupy its own territory. The -- that there were organised rebellions of paramilitary units is another matter. They were trying to secede from that country in contravention of the existing rules and regulations. In other words, the JNA was conducting activities in its own country.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: General, was it ever proposed that the JNA should take over full power and control within the SBWS region?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No, not in relation to that area. But it's well known that at the meeting of the Supreme Command, that is, the Presidency of the SFRY and the military leadership on the 12th of May, 1992, the proposal of the SSNO was considered that in all of Yugoslavia due to the crisis that broke out because illegal arming had been discovered to introduce extraordinary measure, emergency measures, but the Presidency did not accept the proposal. Nor -- nor did the JNA ever try to have emergency measures introduced in any area, including Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment. Mr. Zivanovic, we didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I would suggest that the witness repeat the date. I think that the date in transcript is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: General, you mentioned the date of 12 May 1992. Is that the date you wanted to refer to?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't mean that date, and I didn't say it, but the interpreters probably didn't hear it properly. It is the 12th of March, the session of the Supreme Command. The 12th of March, 1991. And then it was extended afterwards on the 14th and 15th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, that's an important correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: General, did the JNA have forces on the ground in the SBWS that were capable of controlling the whole region of the SBWS?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: At the beginning of your testimony, you referred to an issue regarding mobilisation around the time of the declaration of immediate threat of war. Can you provide some information regarding that issue. What was the problem?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: The problem was that the peacetime levels of the JNA, that is to say, soldiers serving their military service, they were supposed to be released in 1991, in September. This was one of the largest groups of conscripts ever, almost 90.000 soldiers, and this was the highest quality that the JNA had. General Kadijevic suggested to the Presidency that these conscripts have their military service extended because of the military and politician situation in the country. However, the Presidency did not agree with that, and these soldiers were let go, and, therefore, the overall combat readiness of the JNA was significantly decreased. Therefore, the reserve of the JNA was called upon. However, since a state of imminent threat of war or a state of emergency had not been declared, then they were called up under the guise of a military exercise. And according to the then-regulations, they could stay for a maximum of 15 days. Then resistance started. Why were they being called up since they had already attended military exercises before that? Then also some opposition parties joined in, those who wanted to profit politically at that point in time. Then there's the situation in Serbia as such. Serbia says, We're not at war. We cannot mobilise anyone. And those who want to join the JNA voluntarily can do so. This created a create deal of difficulty, in terms of making the JNA capable of dealing with the situation that they were up against, the blockade of barracks, prisoners taken from the ranks of the JNA, and so on. Finally in this situation, only on the 3rd of October, the Presidency made a decision to declare a state of imminent threat of war with a view to legalising mobilisation of the reserve force of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you mentioned that -- that General Kadijevic's proposal regarding the 90.000 conscripts was not accepted, and you have also mentioned the problems with the reserve forces of the JNA. What armed elements ended up going to the SBWS to -- to make up the lack of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, reservists went, those who had been mobilised. Those who had responded to the call-up, that is, because, to a large extent, there were those who didn't want to respond to call-up. That is one thing. Secondly, in such a situation when the JNA is not properly manned, measures were taken to call up volunteers that will become part of the JNA. And on the 13th of September, 1991, the 3rd Administration of the General Staff, wrote a set of instructions or I can perhaps say an order, a guide-line, as to how volunteers should be taken in, those who want to join the JNA. That was the first time to regulate from a normative point of view the taking of volunteers into the JNA, and it happened because there was a lack of personnel within the JNA itself. They also went to JNA units, those who responded to the call-up of JNA. They were sent to the JNA. However, along parallel lines, some political parties, especially the Radical Party, the Serb Radical Party, then the SPO, they brought people together. They carried out a kind of mobilisation, if you will, of some of their members, and they also sent them to the front line. They did not respond -- or, rather, report directly to JNA units. They reported to these local staffs of the Territorial Defence in Slavonia and Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: General, I want to ask you now about a concept about which this Trial Chamber has already heard; namely, the concept of Town Commands. Can you tell us what your understanding is of what a Town Command was under the laws and regulations that applied back in 1991/1992.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I can explain that to the extent to which I know, because that was not within the sector of my own work. I do know, though, that when operations were over in Vukovar the establishment of Town Commands was regulated in a lawful way. The civilian sector of the SSNO wrote a set of instructions as to how these Town Commands should be constituted and what their tasks were. However, we see that there, within that Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, Ljuban Devetak is signing his name as commander of the town. So they established some Town Commands of their own. It was mainly Territorial Defence staffs or Territorial Defence units. However, these were not Town Commands in the sense in which they were later defined in an order issued by the SSNO.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us, what was your understanding of the purpose of a Town Command? And what I mean by that, I mean a legitimate Town Command established within the JNA structure?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to these legal Town Commands, the basic task was to secure peace within the area of responsibility. Furthermore, to help establish local civilian government. That is to say, providing professional assistance to them so that they could start functioning and so that a normal system of life and work could be established for the business community, for all activities. So these Town Commands were not order-issuing authorities. They were not - how shall I put this? - the supreme government in that particular area, they could be that only if a state of emergency were to be declared, not to say occupation or to establish military government. So according to all these instructions, it was stated very specifically what this was all about. It has to do with rendering assistance to these local organs that were supposed to start functioning in the territory where there weren't any war operations anymore. They should establish authority there and normal life on the ground. The only place where Town Commands had direct responsibility was to create lists of military conscripts, to help constitute legal units of the legal Territorial Defence in that area, to help them have war assignments, to know where they should report for equipment and weaponry, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at a document, 65 ter 708. This is tab 112. And Your Honours, this is another document that is pending an exhibit number. And when I mean pending exhibit number, it's pending based upon a decision by this Trial Chamber with regard to a second motion for admissions of documents cited in the Theunens report and those P numbers haven't been assigned yet as of this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: General, what we have in front of us is instructions on conducting the civilian affairs in crisis area by the SSNO, civilian defence sector, and it's dated 25 November, 1991. In your last answer, or last couple of answers, you referenced a set of instructions that were issued. Are these those instructions?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: And you can see that this was immediately done after the Vukovar operations were over.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And could you provide us an explanation of what the role of the SSNO Civilian Defence Sector was with regard to matters such as Town Commands?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as a professional organ of the SSNO, they have an instructive role, if you will. Organisational activity, in terms of helping carry out these tasks, these tasks that were now before the Town Commands. Up here on the stamp you can see that this is an entire sector within the SSNO, by then Sector for Civilian Defence. So there's civilian protection under them and all other problems that have to do with civilian activities, General Pujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What weight was given by the Military Districts to instructions issued by this Civilian Defence Sector?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Since this was a properly regulated army, I don't think there's anything troublesome involved. All the commands and units that received this order, this set of instructions, acted upon it with full responsibility. However, I did not monitor its level of realisation, but I have no doubt in terms of this task being received with full responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at some of the provisions of these instructions. If we could turn to page 3. And this section provides the tasks of the organs for civilian affairs in the commands of JNA units and the Town Commands. And we see under various items listed in the section, tasks -- the tasks frequently referred to co-operating with or assisting the civilian government and administrative organs on various local matters. Is that consistent with your understanding of what a Town Command is?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is it words like "participation," "establishing obligations," "rendering assistance," "direct co-operation." So that shows what the essence of their tasks was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we can turn to page 4 of this document. And if we could look at item number 10, it states: "Direct co-operation with the administrative-executive organs of the state administration for the affairs of the national defence and proposed measures with the aim of efficient functioning of those organs." Can you provide us a little bit more insight into the purpose of this task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it's -- it's over the page, over the page, because I don't need -- I don't read what you just cited from number 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It -- perhaps I misread it. But it's at the -- top of the page, item number 10, "Direct co-operation" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I was at the bottom of the page. Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: General, just looking at this item 10, can you provide us with some insights into what this task entails.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: It entails -- or, rather, this has to do with making the defence system operational in that territory. That is why military departments are being established within the organs of socio-political communities as they were at the time. They are establishing records of military conscripts, according to their specialties; then also establishing units of the Territorial Defence in that area; then units of civilian protection. All of these are tasks that are under these administrative executive organs. Let me take the example of the municipality. These organs from the military commands are in charge of giving direct assistance to these civilian authorities so that they could carry out these activities successfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn -- or, actually, I think, if we could scroll down. And now I want to look towards the bottom. And, in particular, under section 2, item 4 of these instructions state: "Co-operation with the other organs of government, local communities, companies and other organisations and citizens on the protection of lives, personal safety, and security of property ..." And then if we look under item 5, it further states: "Co-ordination of activities and establishing direct co-operation with the organs of the government in preventing and uncovering criminal acts, and discovering and capturing the perpetrators and taking them before the authorised judicial organs." Could you provide us some insights as to the role of Town Commands with regard to law enforcement.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what is highlighted here is co-operation between the military organs and the civilian organs of the interior and joint activities aimed at finding the perpetrators of crime and ensuring peace and security in the area. So this has to do with public law and order and crime prevention. Military organs will be involved in these efforts, in co-operation with the civilian authorities that are supposed to be the mainstays of these activities. So this is co-ordination of tasks on both sides and providing assistance in order to have this start functioning as soon as possible in the field of public safety and security.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I would now like to show you a few more documents relating to this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have on e-court, 65 ter 6046, which is tab 146.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What we have in front of us is a 2nd Proletariat Guards Mechanised Brigade report to the 1st Proletariat Guards Mechanised Division command dated 10 December 1991. General, do you recall the general area in which the 2nd Proletariat Guards Brigade was responsible for in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say anything for sure, but as for the Lovas case, where the detachment of the TO from Lovas was resubordinated to that brigade, I believe that that would be that. But specifically, I don't know what its area of responsibility was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we look under item 3 of this report, it reports that police stations in the zone of responsibility have been formed in accordance with the Serbian MUP regulations and elected authorities. And then if we could look at item 6, which is on the next page of the English, this document reports that the brigade is located in an area where all organs of authority have been functioning from before. General, what does this mean in terms of the JNA's responsibility for law and order in this area?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I see in paragraph 7 it says that an interim assistant for civilian affairs has been appointed and he has the rank of major. So the brigade was issued a specific task in relation to Town Commands that are supposed to help the successful functioning of state organs in the territory. What he is invoking is that the staff of the TO is established as were TO Staffs in Serbia. And then also other organs function according to the same principle, like in Serbia. So there shouldn't be any major problems in terms of carrying out these tasks -- these tasks, because all of that is already functioning successfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And in your last answer, you reference the TO Staffs were established, and I just want to correct you. The document actually refers to -- to -- to police stations having been established in this area. And that's why my question was with regard to law enforcement at this stage with the establishment of functioning police stations in this area, what did that mean in terms of the role of Town Commands?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Down here he himself says that he won't have any major obligations there because the entire system is already functioning according to the one in place in the Republic of Serbia. For me to be able to interpret this more specifically, I would need to know what his area of responsibility is because I don't know whether perhaps the territory of Serbia, that part around Sid is part of his area of responsibility, or is it just this SAO, or rather, the territory of Croatia? So these are two separate things. If he is in the territory of Serb, the system is functioning. If he is in the territorial where that is not the case, then it is a good thing that these organs have already started functioning and have been doing so for quite a while and that civilians rule has been established in the area, then he doesn't have any major obligations in that respect. That is his interpretation because everything had already been resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall, General, any problems with the establishment of police stations in the Republic of Serbia during this time-period?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No. Those stations existed and there weren't any changes, radical changes that were taking place. I am not aware of them having any problems in Serbia with the functioning of police stations. I'm not aware of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And are you aware of any Town Commands being established in the Republic of Serbia during this period?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Olmsted. General Vasiljevic, this is the end of the hearing for today. You are not released as a witness. We expect you back tomorrow morning at 9.00, and that means that you are not allowed to discuss your testimony with anybody, and it also means that you are not allowed to talk to any of the parties. If that is clear, the Court Usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may tender the last document into evidence, 65 ter 6046.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2924.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Court adjourned.
